core: The Great Depression was the longest and deepest economic downturn in the history of the United States and the modern industrial economy, beginning in 1929 and ending during World War II in 1941 (Federal Reserve History dates the contraction from August 1929).

The 1929 stock market crash was the dramatic trigger: on 'Black Thursday,' October 24, 1929, the New York Stock Exchange lost 11 percent of its value; on 'Black Tuesday,' October 29, 1929, holders traded over sixteen million shares and lost over $14 billion in a single day; the market lost almost one-half its value in the fall of 1929.

Economists and historians distinguish the crash (a trigger) from the deeper causes and weigh those causes differently: a speculative stock bubble fueled by buying 'on margin' (borrowed money); a banking system that collapsed and a money supply that contracted; overproduction and underconsumption; deep inequality; and international strains including war debts, the gold standard, and tariffs.

The Federal Reserve's monetary policy is a central point of debate: from the fall of 1930 through the winter of 1933 the money supply fell by nearly 30 percent, producing severe deflation; economists such as Milton Friedman and Ben Bernanke argue the Fed's failure to stop this deepened the Depression.

The human toll: at the 1933 peak, 24.9% of the workforce (about 12.83 million people) was unemployed (FDR Presidential Library); waves of bank failures wiped out savings; homelessness spread (shantytowns nicknamed 'Hoovervilles'); breadlines and soup kitchens became common.

The Dust Bowl: overproduction and overuse of Great Plains farmland combined with severe drought produced enormous dust storms in the 1930s, ruining farms and driving displaced families (nicknamed 'Okies') westward.

The government response was Franklin D. Roosevelt's New Deal, organized around 'relief, recovery, and reform': the Civilian Conservation Corps (CCC, 1933), the Works Progress Administration (WPA, 1935), the Social Security Act (1935), and financial regulation including the Glass-Steagall Banking Act of 1933 (which created the FDIC) and federal securities laws (1933-1934) that created the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The New Deal's effectiveness is genuinely debated: it provided relief and lasting reforms and reduced unemployment from its 1933 peak, but did not by itself restore full employment; critics on the right attacked the growth of federal spending and power, critics on the left said it did not go far enough, and a 1937-38 'double-dip' recession interrupted recovery. Full recovery in output and employment came with mobilization for World War II (1941).
supporting: Only about 10 percent of American households owned stock, yet the crash and ensuing depression cost nearly a third of Americans their savings and jobs, because over 90 percent of banks had themselves invested in the market.
Within a year of the crash, U.S. gross national product declined by over 25 percent and unemployment tripled from 1.5 million (end of 1929) to 4.5 million.
March 1933 was the low point: the commercial banking system collapsed and, within 48 hours of his inauguration, Roosevelt declared a national bank holiday; the Emergency Banking Act of 1933 followed.
Distinguishing established fact (what happened, when) from interpretation (why it happened and how well the New Deal worked) is the core historical-thinking skill this topic teaches.

claims.claim: The stock market crash usually treated as the trigger of the Great Depression occurred in October 1929, with 'Black Thursday' on October 24 (the NYSE lost 11 percent of its value) and 'Black Tuesday' on October 29 (over sixteen million shares traded, over $14 billion lost in a day); the market lost almost half its value that fall.
Buying 'on margin' meant purchasing stock with a small down payment and borrowed money, intending to sell at a higher price before the balance came due; this fueled a speculative bubble in the 1920s.

The crash was a trigger, not the sole cause: only about 10 percent of households owned stock, yet over 90 percent of banks had invested in the market, so bank failures spread the collapse; within a year GNP fell over 25 percent and unemployment tripled from 1.5 to 4.5 million.

The Great Depression was the longest and deepest downturn in U.S. history, beginning in 1929 (contraction from August 1929) and ending during World War II in 1941, with the low point in March 1933 when the banking system collapsed and Roosevelt declared a national bank holiday.

From the fall of 1930 through the winter of 1933 the U.S. money supply fell by nearly 30 percent, producing severe deflation; economists including Ben Bernanke have argued the Federal Reserve's failure to prevent this deepened the Depression.
At the height of the Depression in 1933, 24.9% of the total workforce, about 12,830,000 people, was unemployed.
The Dust Bowl resulted from overproduction and overuse of Great Plains land plus severe drought, producing epic dust storms that ruined farms and drove displaced families (the 'Okies') westward.

Roosevelt's New Deal was organized around relief, recovery, and reform and included the Civilian Conservation Corps (1933), the Works Progress Administration (1935), the Social Security Act (1935), and financial regulation such as the Glass-Steagall Banking Act of 1933, which created the FDIC and insured personal deposits.

The New Deal's effectiveness is genuinely debated: conservatives objected to expanded federal spending and power while liberals said it did not do enough; a 1937 double-dip recession interrupted recovery, and full recovery in output and employment came only with mobilization for World War II.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How effective was the New Deal, and when did recovery occur?
positions: The New Deal provided essential relief and durable reforms (deposit insurance, Social Security, securities regulation) and cut unemployment from its 1933 peak
Monetarist and other critics argue Federal Reserve and policy errors, not just structural weakness, deepened and prolonged the slump; the 1937-38 recession shows recovery was incomplete
Contemporary critics on the right attacked federal spending and power; critics on the left said the New Deal did too little
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson states the established facts (programs, dates, the 1933 unemployment peak, the 1937 double-dip, recovery with WWII in 1941) and presents the effectiveness question as an open scholarly and political debate rather than declaring one side correct.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Weighting of the causes of the Depression
positions: Monetary explanations emphasize the ~30% fall in the money supply and Fed inaction
Keynesian and structural explanations emphasize underconsumption, overproduction, and inequality
International explanations emphasize the gold standard, war debts, and tariffs
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson lists the major cited causes and states explicitly that economists and historians weigh them differently, attributing the monetary-contraction figure to Federal Reserve History.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft was pure boilerplate ('Great Depression is a foundational concept in History...') with no substantive historical or economic claims; none of it was reused.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced placeholder scope with a substantive lesson on the 1929 crash, the debated causes, the human toll (unemployment, bank failures, Dust Bowl), the New Deal, and recovery with WWII.
Attributed the 24.9% (1933 peak) unemployment figure to the FDR Presidential Library and dated it; attributed the ~30% money-supply contraction to Federal Reserve History.
Presented the New Deal-effectiveness question and the weighting of causes as genuine debates rather than settled fact.
